transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, to be honest, it’s... it’s just been a really overwhelming couple of weeks. I work as a mechanic at this auto shop downtown, mostly dealing with heavy-duty stuff, you know, trucks, SUVs, that kind of thing. I've been there a while and I know my way around a garage, but... well, what brought me in is that I keep hearing this voice. 

It’s a man’s voice. And I know how that sounds, but it’s not like a faint thought in my head or just my imagination playing tricks on me. It is as clear as somebody standing right next to me holding a socket wrench. I'll be working in my bay, just trying to get my hours in, and I hear him coming straight out of the garage vents. We have these massive industrial vents up near the ceiling for the exhaust fumes, and his voice just travels right down through the metal. Or sometimes—and this is the part that really messes with my head—I’ll pop the hood on a vehicle to check an alternator or do a routine inspection, and the voice comes right from under the hood. Just... right out of the engine bay. 

And he just talks and talks. He keeps telling me not to trust my husband, just going on about how my husband is plotting things and I need to watch my back with him. And then he’ll switch and start telling me not to touch certain cars. Like, the service advisor will roll a car into my bay for a diagnostic, and the voice will tell me I absolutely cannot touch that specific car, like it's dangerous or something. It’s making it impossible to do my job because I'm just standing there staring at a manifold, listening to this guy tell me my marriage is a lie and I can't do my work, and... I just don't know how to make it stop.
Does the voice ever tell you to do something, rather than just telling you not to do something or warning you about your husband?

No, no, it’s not really like that. He doesn't say... you know, he doesn't give me orders to go out and actually do things. It’s always about what I shouldn't do, or what I need to watch out for. It’s like this constant, heavy blanket of... of warnings, just suffocating me. 

Like, I’ll be standing there, wiping my hands on a shop towel, just trying to take a five-minute breather between jobs, and he’s not saying "go confront your husband" or "go smash that windshield." It’s more like... "don't go home tonight, he's waiting for you, he's got a plan." And it just spins and spins in my head. I mean, my husband and I have been married for five years, and sure, we have our normal couples stuff, but this voice makes me analyze every single little thing the man does. Did he leave his keys on the kitchen counter because he's rushing to hide something from me? The voice says yes, absolutely, do not trust him, do not eat the dinner he made. 

And at the shop, it's the exact same restrictive thing. It's never "cut the brake lines." It's "don't touch that F-150, if you touch that F-150, something terrible is going to happen." And I try to argue back sometimes, just in my head, like, "Look, I have to do this, it's on my ticket for the day, the service manager is literally waiting for the diagnostic code," but the voice just talks right over me. He has this really deep, booming tone, especially when it echoes out of the vents, and he just keeps repeating these warnings, over and over, until I'm just paralyzed standing there by my toolbox. I'll just be staring at my socket sets, completely frozen. So, no, he doesn't tell me to *do* things... it's just... it's always pulling me away from living my life, if that makes sense. It's just constant roadblocks.
Do you ever feel like you're outside of your body watching yourself, or like things aren't real?

No, I... I don't think so. I mean, I've heard people talk about that kind of thing, like on TV or whatever, where they float above themselves or feel like they're in a dream, but... no, everything feels completely real to me. Too real, honestly. 

Like, when I'm at the shop, I feel the grease on my hands, I smell the oil and the exhaust, I feel the cold metal of the wrenches. I'm definitely in my body. And my house, when I go home to my husband, the house is real, the tension is real. I don't feel like I'm watching a movie of my life or anything like that. I'm right there in the middle of it. It's just that I have this voice talking to me while I'm in the middle of it. 

I guess sometimes I might zone out a bit, just because I'm so focused on what the voice is saying, like I mentioned before when I just freeze by my toolbox. The guys at the shop probably think I'm daydreaming or something, but I'm not disconnected from reality. I'm just trapped in this very specific, very loud reality where this guy is constantly warning me about everything. But my body is mine, and I'm definitely inside it, feeling every single bit of the stress. It's exhausting, being so present for all of it, you know? I kind of wish I could just float away sometimes, just to get a break from the noise, but... no, I'm stuck right here. Everything is just solid and heavy and... real.
Do you ever see things that aren't there, like shadows or figures, when you're alone or in a crowded space?

No, no, I don't see anything. It's not like that. I don't see shadows or ghosts or people who aren't there, whether I'm by myself in the bays or if I'm walking through a crowded grocery store. My vision is perfectly fine, you know? I need it to be, to do my job. You can't exactly miss a cracked belt or a leaking seal when you're under a chassis. So, no, nothing with my eyes. 

But like I was saying before, the main thing—the whole reason I even made this appointment and came in here today—is that voice. That man's voice. That's the part that's so overwhelming. Because I don't see him, but I hear him as clearly as I'm hearing you right now. It's just... it's so distinct. Like I told you, it comes right out of those massive metal exhaust vents up on the ceiling at the shop. The acoustics in a garage are already crazy, you know, with the impact wrenches and the air compressors going off, but his voice just cuts right through all of that, echoing down the metal ductwork. 

And then, of course, there's the times when it comes from under the hood of a car. I'll be leaning over the engine block, maybe checking the fluid levels or inspecting a radiator hose, and the voice is just right there, coming from the engine bay, clear as day. And he just keeps going on and on about how my husband is plotting against me, telling me I can't trust him, and then switching to telling me I absolutely cannot touch certain cars that get rolled into my bay. But I never *see* him. There's no figure standing there. I'll look around, I'll check under the lift, I'll look up at the vents, but there's nobody there. It's just the voice, but it's so real and so loud that I don't even need to see him to know he's right there, messing with my life.
Do you find it hard to keep track of what you're saying or to express your thoughts in a way that makes sense to others?

No, I... I don't think so. I mean, I feel like I'm explaining things pretty clearly, right? I'm telling you exactly what's going on with the voice and the shop and my husband. I don't feel like I lose my train of thought or anything like that. 

I mean, sure, sometimes when I'm talking to the service manager at work, I might get a little distracted, but that's only because the voice is literally booming out of the vents right over his head while he's trying to hand me a work order. Like, he'll be standing there talking about a timing belt replacement on a Honda, and the whole time, that deep voice is just echoing down the ductwork, telling me not to touch the car, warning me about my husband. So, yeah, maybe I pause for a second, or maybe I have to ask the manager to repeat himself, but it's not because I can't keep track of my own thoughts. It's because I'm trying to listen to two people at once, and one of them is incredibly loud and won't shut up. 

But as far as my actual thoughts, and how I talk? No, I think I make perfect sense. I've always been good at explaining things. You have to be, in my line of work. You have to be able to explain to a customer exactly why their transmission is slipping, or why their brake pads are worn down to the rotors, and you have to do it in a way they understand, you know? You can't just throw a bunch of technical jargon at them. So I'm used to organizing my thoughts and communicating clearly. 

Even with my husband, when we argue—and we do argue, especially lately, with everything the voice is telling me about him—I know exactly what I'm saying. I lay it all out for him. I tell him, "Look, I know you're hiding something, I know you have a plan," and I don't stumble over my words. I just... I say what I mean. I guess sometimes people might look at me a little funny, like the guys at the shop when I freeze up by my toolbox, but that's just because they don't know what I'm dealing with. They don't hear what I hear. If they did, they'd understand exactly why I act the way I do. But my speech itself? No, it's fine. I'm completely tracking with everything I'm saying to you right now. I just have a lot to explain, because there's a lot going on, and I need you to understand exactly how overwhelming this voice is.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

Yeah, I... I guess I have. I mean, it's hard to explain, but it's like... it's like the color has just drained out of everything, you know? Like, I used to love going to church on Sundays. I was always the one organizing the potlucks, making sure everyone brought a dish, setting up the tables in the fellowship hall. I loved that. I loved the community, the chatting, the feeling of being involved and doing something good. But lately? Lately, I just... I can't even make myself care. 

There are these long stretches where I don't even go. I just skip the potlucks entirely. People will call me, you know, the ladies from church leaving voicemails, asking where I've been, if I'm still bringing my potato salad, and I just... I don't call anyone back. I stare at my phone while it rings, and I just can't muster the energy to pick it up. It feels like such a monumental effort just to say hello. 

And it's not just church. It's everything. Even at work, which I used to take so much pride in. I mean, I'm a good mechanic. I love the satisfaction of fixing a problem, of getting an engine running smooth again. But now, I'll just sit there in the bay, or even at home in my living room, and I'll just stare. Like, I'll literally just sit and stare at my tools, my ratchets and my torque wrenches, and I just feel nothing. I can't make myself care about the cars, I can't make myself care about the church, I can't even make myself care about calling my friends back. It's just this heavy, blank feeling. It's like I'm hollowed out. And honestly, it's terrifying, because I know I should care, I know I used to care, but the feeling is just... gone. It's just completely gone, and I don't know how to get it back.
Do you find that your thoughts are racing or difficult to follow when you're trying to think clearly?

No, I wouldn't say they race. It's not like... it's not like a bunch of cars zooming by on a track, if that's what you mean. My thoughts are actually really methodical. When I'm in the bay, even with everything else going on, even with that voice echoing out of the vents and telling me all those things about my husband, my actual thought process is very step-by-step. 

Like, if I'm diagnosing a misfire on a Chevy Silverado, I don't just jump all over the place. I hook up the scanner, I pull the codes, I check the spark plugs, I test the ignition coils, I look at the fuel injectors. I go right down the list, one by one. You can't have racing thoughts when you're doing diagnostics, especially electrical work, you know? You have to trace the wire from the battery to the fuse box to the component. If your mind is jumping all over the place and you can't follow your own thoughts, you're gonna fry a module or tell a customer they need a five-hundred-dollar part when it was just a bad ground wire. 

So no, my thoughts don't race at all. They just focus on what's in front of me, or... well, they focus on the voice because it's so loud I can't ignore it. But it's not a jumble in my head. It's not moving too fast to catch. If anything, it's the exact opposite lately. Like I was saying about that heavy, blank feeling... it's more like my brain gets stuck in the mud rather than racing like a sports car. When I'm sitting there in my living room, just staring at my tools for hours, my mind isn't spinning with a million different ideas. It's just... empty. It's just completely blank. So, no, definitely not racing. I almost wish they would race, just a little bit, maybe then I could snap out of this funk and actually care about something again, but they don't. They just plod along, or they just stop entirely.
Do you feel any strong emotions, like fear or anxiety, when you hear the voice?

Well, yeah, I mean, absolutely I feel anxious. It's terrifying. Actually, that's the whole reason I'm here. What brought me in is that I just can't take the fear of it anymore, because I keep hearing this man’s voice, and it's so incredibly real. 

I know I mentioned it echoing out of the garage vents, but it's not just up in the ceiling. Sometimes I'll pull a car into the bay, pop the latch, and lift the hood to do a basic inspection, and the voice is coming from right under the hood. Right there in the engine compartment! And it is as clear as somebody standing right next to me. It's not a whisper, it's not the wind, it's a grown man speaking directly to me while I'm holding my wrench. 

And the things he says... of course they make me anxious. He's constantly telling me not to trust my husband, saying all these things that make me second-guess my entire marriage, making me afraid to even go home at the end of my shift. And then, on top of that, he'll start telling me not to touch certain cars. I'll be reaching in to check a power steering pump, and this clear, deep voice from right next to the radiator will just command me to step away. How am I supposed to not feel fear when that happens? I just freeze up. My heart starts pounding out of my chest, my hands get sweaty, and I just stand there staring at the engine block because I don't know what will happen if I actually touch the car after he warned me not to. 

So, yes, it causes a massive amount of anxiety. I can't work, I can't trust my husband, I can't even open a hood without bracing myself for what this man is going to say to me. It's just completely taken over my day-to-day life, and I couldn't handle the panic anymore, which is exactly why I finally made the appointment to come in.
Have you experienced any traumatic events in your past?

No, I mean... when you say traumatic, I usually think of, like, being in a war, or being in some horrible, catastrophic car wreck. And I've seen the aftermath of some really bad wrecks towed into the shop, believe me. Just last year, we had this Ford Explorer brought in that was completely crushed on the driver's side, just folded up like an accordion. The tow truck driver told me the guy somehow walked away without a scratch, which is an absolute miracle when you looked at the frame damage. But me personally? No. I've never been in a crash like that. 

I actually had a pretty standard, normal life, I guess. I grew up, went to school, did a couple of years at the community college before I finally just admitted to myself that sitting at a desk in a classroom wasn't for me. I just liked working with my hands too much, you know? My dad was always tinkering out in the garage when I was a kid, and I'd always be right out there with him, holding the flashlight. He'd always get frustrated and yell at me to hold it steady—you know how dads are, always saying, "Keep the light on the bolt, not in my eyes!"—but that's not trauma. That's just growing up. My parents were good to me. I was never abused or assaulted or anything terrible like that. 

And my husband and I, well, at least before all this stuff with the voice started making me doubt everything, we had a really quiet, ordinary life together. We met, we dated, we got married, we bought our little house. Nothing crazy has ever happened to me. I've never even broken a bone, which is honestly kind of surprising considering I work around heavy machinery and two-ton vehicles on hydraulic lifts all day. 

So, I don't know. I sit here and I try to rack my brain, trying to think if there's some hidden, awful thing in my past that would explain all this. Like, I keep wondering if there's a reason why my brain feels so heavy and empty, or why there's suddenly a grown man's voice coming out from under the hood of a Honda Civic telling me my husband is a liar. But... there's just nothing. My life was completely normal. Boring, even! It was just church, the shop, and home. So no, no trauma. Honestly, a part of me almost wishes there was something, because then at least there would be a reason for why this is happening to me, you know? Like a cause and effect. But no, I haven't been through anything like that.
Do you believe the voice you're hearing is real and actually coming from the vents or under the hood of cars?

Well, yeah... I mean, I know I just brought all that up, but yes, I absolutely believe it's real. Because it is real. I'm not... I'm not just making it up or imagining it like a daydream, if that's what you're getting at. 

You have to understand, when you work in a service bay, you get used to a very specific set of noises. You've got pneumatic impact wrenches going off, air compressors kicking on, the bay doors rattling, radios blaring... you learn how to filter out the background noise so you can hear the important stuff, like a rod knocking or a bearing whining. But this voice... it cuts right through all of that shop noise. Like I was explaining, it's the whole reason I'm sitting here talking to you. I keep hearing this man’s voice, and it's not some fuzzy thought in the back of my mind. It has a physical location. 

When it comes from the garage vents, I can literally hear the acoustics of it, like the sound waves are bouncing off the galvanized steel of the ductwork. And when I pop a hood and it's coming from the engine bay... I mean, it is as clear as somebody standing right next to me. Clearer, honestly, because half the guys I work with mumble. But this man doesn't mumble. He speaks with total authority. When he's telling me not to trust my husband, or when he's explicitly warning me not to touch certain cars, I can hear the pitch of his voice, the tone, even the breath behind the words. 

If it wasn't real, how could I hear it so clearly over a running engine? How could it startle me so badly that I physically drop my ratchet? People think that if you hear something that isn't supposed to be there, it must feel like a dream. But it doesn't. It's solid. It's as real as the grease on my hands. I've actually caught myself walking circles around a vehicle, checking the blind spots around the hydraulic lift, looking behind the big Snap-on toolboxes, because I am completely convinced there is a physical human being hiding in my work area playing a sick joke on me. But there's never anyone there. It's just the voice. 

But it's coming from right there, right out of the intake manifold or the radiator fan, just plain as day, telling me all these awful things. So, yes, doctor, I believe it's real. I have to believe it's real because my own two ears are hearing it happen, shift after shift. I wouldn't be taking time off work and sitting in a psychiatrist's office if I didn't know for a fact that I was really hearing it.
Have you ever used recreational drugs or alcohol to the point where it interfered with your daily life?

Oh, no. No, definitely not. I mean, I know there's this whole stereotype about mechanics, right? People think we all just clock out at five, crack open a twelve-pack of cheap beer, and sit around on overturned buckets in the parking lot until the sun goes down. And, sure, I've worked with a couple of guys over the years who... well, let's just say they smelled a little like a distillery on Monday mornings, and the service manager usually had to have a closed-door talk with them. But me? No, absolutely not. I don't mess with drugs at all, never have. And alcohol? I mean, maybe I'll have a beer if we're at a summer barbecue or something, but never, ever to the point where it messes with my life or my job. 

You have to understand, my line of work is incredibly dangerous. I'm standing under vehicles that weigh thousands of pounds, suspended in the air by hydraulic lifts. I'm dealing with highly pressurized lines, volatile chemicals, and heavy machinery. If you are hungover, or high, or even just a little fuzzy from a few too many drinks the night before, you could literally kill yourself or someone else in the bay next to you. You miss one safety latch on the hoist, or you forget to torque a lug nut to the right spec, and it's an absolute disaster waiting to happen. So I take that really, really seriously. I've always been super strict with myself about being completely clear-headed when I walk onto that shop floor. 

Which is honestly why this whole thing with the voice is so incredibly terrifying to me, because I *am* sober! I'm completely, one-hundred-percent sober, and I'm still hearing this man talking to me from the engine compartments! If I was on drugs, or if I was some heavy drinker, at least I could just blame it on that, you know? Like, I could just say, 'Oh, I took a bad pill, or I drank way too much whiskey, and that's why the Honda Civic is telling me my husband is a liar.' It would make sense! But I don't even smoke weed! I just drink my coffee—usually black, from the terrible drip machine in the breakroom that never gets cleaned—and I do my work. 

So no, drugs and alcohol are definitely not the issue here. I don't have any kind of substance problem. I almost wish I did, because then you could just tell me to go to rehab and this whole nightmare would stop. But I'm completely clean, and it's still happening anyway.
Do you think the voice is coming from inside your own mind or from an external source?

Well, like I was trying to explain before... it is definitely external. I mean, it is absolutely coming from outside of my own body. If it was just in my mind, wouldn't it sound like my own thoughts? You know, like when you read a book to yourself and you hear your own voice in your head? But this isn't that. This is a man. A grown man. 

And honestly, that's exactly what brought me in here, why I finally made this appointment. I just keep hearing this man's voice, and it has a physical location in the room. It's coming right out of the garage vents. And sometimes, I'll pop the latch on a customer's vehicle and it's coming from right under the hood, bouncing off the engine block. It is as clear as somebody standing right next to me, handing me a wrench. 

It's not some fuzzy echo in my brain, it's... it's out there in the air with me. I can hear the sound waves hitting the concrete floors and the metal tool cabinets. And the things he says are just so specific and demanding. He's constantly telling me not to trust my husband, which, like I said, is driving me crazy because my husband and I have always had a good, normal life, but this voice is just so insistent that he's lying to me. And then he'll explicitly warn me not to touch certain cars in the bay. I'll be walking up to do a standard brake job or something, and the voice will just project right out of the grill, telling me to stay away from it. 

If it was inside my head, I wouldn't be walking around the shop trying to find the guy, right? I wouldn't be checking behind the tire balancer or staring up into the ceiling grates with my flashlight. I'm looking because the sound is physically hitting my eardrums from a specific direction. So, yeah, it's external. It has to be external. I just... I don't know how he's doing it, or how he's hiding from me, but it's definitely not my own mind. It's a real voice, out loud, in the shop.
Do you often find yourself having trouble expressing your thoughts in a coherent and logical manner?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I know I'm talking a lot right now, and I know I have a tendency to really get into the weeds with the details, but... no, I don't have trouble making sense. My thoughts are perfectly logical. They have to be, you know? 

In my line of work, if you can't explain your diagnostic process clearly, you're not going to last very long. Like, if I'm doing an inspection and I find that the brake calipers are seizing up, I can't just go to the service writer and spout a bunch of jumbled nonsense. I have to explain exactly what I found, step by step, so they can translate that to the customer and get the repair authorized. I have to be able to say, look, the slide pins are rusted out, the pads are wearing unevenly because of it, and the rotor is completely glazed, so we need to replace the whole assembly. It has to be a straight line from A to B to C. 

So my brain works in a very systematic way. I'm always putting things in order. Even with everything going on right now, with this man's voice yelling at me from the radiators and the stress it's putting on me, I feel like I'm laying it all out for you very clearly, aren't I? I'm not... I'm not losing my train of thought or speaking in riddles or anything like that. I know exactly what I want to say, and I say it. It's just that I have a lot to say right now because this whole situation with the voice is so incredibly overwhelming and it's taking up so much of my energy. 

But as far as being coherent? Yeah, I'm definitely coherent. Anyone at the shop would tell you I'm probably the most thorough person there when it comes to explaining a problem. I might give you more information than you asked for, like my husband always teases me about, but it always makes sense. It's always logical.
Have you ever had an experience like this before, where you heard voices or had other unusual perceptions?

No, never. I mean, before this started? Absolutely not. I had a completely normal life. I've never had any weird perceptions, or heard anything that wasn't there, or experienced anything even remotely like this in my entire life. 

But this current situation... the voices and the tracking beliefs, they've been happening for about ten months now. And I say tracking beliefs because I know how it sounds to other people, but I am absolutely certain someone is keeping tabs on my location and following my movements. But yeah, all of it—the voice in the shop, the feeling that I'm being monitored and tracked—it's been about ten solid months. 

I know the timeline exactly because I remember the exact week it started. It was right at the tail end of winter, right as we were finally getting out of the rush of swapping out snow tires and moving into spring maintenance. I was doing a heater core replacement on a 2015 Chevy Silverado—which, if you know anything about modern trucks, means you basically have to pull the entire dashboard out just to get to it, it is a massive, incredibly frustrating job that takes hours. I was deep under the dash, my hands were cramped, and that was the very first time I heard the man's voice. And it was right around that exact same time that I started noticing the signs that I was being tracked, like someone was monitoring my route home from the garage. 

So it's been ten months of this. And ten months might not sound like a long time in the grand scheme of a whole life, but when you are going to work every single day and you feel like you have to check the wheel wells of your own truck for GPS monitors, and you have a man yelling out of a radiator that your husband is a liar... ten months feels like an absolute eternity. I haven't had a single moment of real peace since it started. I'm just exhausted. But before that Silverado ten months ago? No. Never. Nothing like this ever happened to me before.
Have you ever had any other episodes in your life where you heard voices or saw things that weren't there?

Well, like I was just saying a minute ago... no, nothing else besides what's happening right now. I don't see things, if that's what you're asking. But this... this is exactly what brought me in here today. I just keep hearing this man’s voice, and like I mentioned, it’s coming right out of the garage vents. Or sometimes I'll be doing an inspection and it's coming from right under the hood of whatever I'm working on. 

And I really need you to understand, it's as clear as somebody standing right next to me. It's not a whisper. It's like a coworker standing shoulder-to-shoulder with me in the bay, just talking right into my ear. And he's just constantly telling me not to trust my husband, which really messes with my head because I love my husband, and then telling me not to touch certain cars. He'll just randomly decide a vehicle is off-limits and loudly warn me to stay away from it while I'm trying to do my job. 

So no, I haven't had any other episodes in my past, and I've never seen things that aren't there... it's just this one man, in the shop, doing exactly what I just explained to you. It's just the vents, the engines, and him talking about my husband and the cars. That's the whole reason I finally made this appointment.
Have you ever had any other episodes in your life where you heard voices or had other unusual perceptions that were not related to the current voice you're hearing?

I feel like we're just spinning our tires here, doc. Like I just said, no. There is nothing else. No other episodes, no other voices from five years ago or ten years ago. Just this. 

The entire reason I am sitting in this office taking time away from a very busy shop—and we are incredibly backed up right now, we have three engine swaps waiting on bays—is because I just keep hearing this one specific man's voice. That's it. It's coming from the garage vents, or like I was explaining, sometimes from right under the hood of the cars I'm working on. I'll pop the hood on a sedan and the sound is just bouncing right off the firewall, clear as somebody standing right next to me holding a wrench. 

It's just him. It's not a chorus of people, it's not something from my childhood, it is just him, and he just keeps telling me not to trust my husband, which I've already told you is incredibly distressing to me, or he tells me not to touch certain cars on the lot. I don't have a history of anything else. I've never had any other unusual perceptions or whatever you want to call them. It is literally just this one guy, in the shop, doing this right now, making it impossible for me to just do my job in peace. I don't know how many different ways I can explain it to you, but there's nothing else besides him.
Do you have any family members who have been diagnosed with a mental health condition?

No, not that I know of. I mean, nobody in my family has ever talked about anything like that. We're not really the type of family to sit around and discuss our feelings or, you know, mental health stuff. My dad was a mechanic, too, actually—that's how I got into the business. I grew up in his shop, basically handing him wrenches since I was old enough to walk. He was a hard worker, real old-school, you know? The kind of guy who would work a twelve-hour shift, come home with grease permanently stained into his knuckles, eat dinner, and fall asleep in his recliner watching the news. He never complained, never talked about being stressed or anything. 

And my mom, she was a stay-at-home mom for a long time, then worked part-time at a local bakery. She was always busy, always doing something, keeping the house spotless, making sure we all had what we needed. She was a bit of a worrier, I guess, always fretting about whether we were eating enough vegetables or if the house was clean enough for company, but just normal mom stuff, you know? Nothing that you'd call a diagnosis. 

I have a younger brother, too, but he's out in Colorado working in construction. He's doing great, married, got a couple of kids. We text every now and then, but he's never mentioned anything about seeing a doctor for his head. 

So, yeah, as far as I know, it's just me dealing with... whatever this is. Nobody else in the family has ever had to go to a doctor for hearing voices or thinking they're being tracked. We're just regular, working-class people. We fix things, we build things, we just put our heads down and get the job done. That's why this is all so frustrating for me, because I just want to get back to doing my job without all this interference. But no, no family history of anything like that.
